topics.title: 9.2.1 Understanding Automatic Storage Duration
topics.summary: Ordinary local objects usually have automatic storage duration: their storage is managed as execution enters and leaves the relevant block. Construction establishes the object’s lifetime, and destruction ends it for class objects. The standard’s storage-duration model is more precise than saying every local variable is physically on a stack; optimization can change placement or eliminate storage entirely.

topics.summary: Can a name be local while its object persists? Yes. A function-local static has a local name and persistent storage duration.

cards.question: Can a name be local while its object persists?
cards.answer: Yes. A function-local static has a local name and persistent storage duration.

cards.question: Does a reference universally extend lifetime?
cards.answer: No. Some language constructs have specific extension rules, but a reference is not a general ownership mechanism.

cards.question: Why can returning a value be safer than returning a reference?
cards.answer: The caller receives a result without needing the callee’s local object to remain alive. A reference requires a valid longer-lived target.

cards.question: Why is changing a local to static not always a proper fix?
cards.answer: It changes sharing, persistence, and possibly concurrency behavior. A lifetime extension must still match the application’s intended state model.
